newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-PELE GETS PRESIDENTIAL BACKING FOR SOCCER BILL.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PELE GETS PRESIDENTIAL BACKING FOR SOCCER BILL.

text.p: Pele got presidential backing on Thursday for his attempt to reform Brazilian soccer despite a warning that the world champions could miss out on the 1998 World Cup as a consequence of the measures.
Pele, Brazil's sports minister, has drawn up a bill which would drastically reduce the powers of the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF).

But Joao Havelange, the Brazilian president of world soccer governing body Fifa, warned on Wednesday that Brazil would be suspended or expelled if the bill becomes law because some of its contents infringe Fifa statutes.
On Thursday, the government appeared unmoved by Havelange's ultimatum.
"President Fernando Henrique Cardoso reiterates his total backing for the minister's initiative," said a statement issued by the presidential press office on Thursday.
Pele, who presented the bill to Cardoso on Tuesday, said he would not back down.

"I think it is a big mistake by him," said Pele, referring to Havelange's threat. "We have reached a moment when we do not want to accept these impositions any more. We are not living in a dictatorship."
"I think that it would be a joke if Brazil, which has won four World Cups on the pitch, were to miss a World Cup because of this."
Congressman Severino Alves said: "I don't think this (Havelange's threat) will affect Congress."
Havelange, however, was adamant: "I would ask him (Pele) to reflect on this and see that he has taken a step in the wrong direction."
Asked if Brazil could miss the next World Cup if the bill becomes law before then, Havelange said: "Yes, Brazil could."
There is deep dissatisfaction in Brazil with the way the domestic game is being run.

The CBF, whose president Ricardo Teixeira is Havelange's son-in-law, suffered a severe blow to its credibility in June when it reinstated Fluminense and Bragantino to the national championship, even though they were relegated last year.
As a result, the national championship has 26 teams and fixtures are piling up. Ironically, Fluminense are again candidates for relegation.
The CBF was also hit by a corruption scandal which resulted in Ivens Mendes, former president of its refereeing department, being banned for life from any soccer-related activity.
Teixeira himself was not incriminated but admitted he had given too much power to Mendes.
Teixeira has also been under fire for allowing Atletico Paranaense, who were suspended for one year in the wake of the scandal, to take part in the Brazilian championship.
Congressman Jose Arruda commented: "The one thing we can't do is leave Brazilian soccer as it is."
